scenes.narration: A rent of one point two five billion dollars a month. That is what one artificial intelligence company agreed to pay SpaceX, until May twenty twenty-nine, according to the prospectus SpaceX filed when it went public. Not for a rocket launch. For computer chips.

In twenty twenty-six, SpaceX finally opened its books. And the most famous rocket company in the world turned out to earn most of its money from something else. In its latest quarter, artificial intelligence came first, internet subscriptions second, and rockets last.
So how does SpaceX actually make money? And why has the rocket business, the part everyone watches, been losing money?
By the end of this video, you will know where SpaceX's money comes from, why most of its rockets carry its own cargo, and who really controls the company.

scenes.narration: On June twelfth, twenty twenty-six, SpaceX began trading on the stock market. The shares were sold at one hundred and thirty-five dollars each, and the company, a Texas corporation, raised about eighty-five point seven billion dollars after fees. At that price, by our calculation, the whole company was valued at about one point seven seven trillion dollars.

There is one catch. Before going public, SpaceX bought xAI, the artificial intelligence company that also owns the social network X. Both were controlled by Elon Musk. So the filings rewrite SpaceX's past to include them. On that basis, revenue in twenty twenty-five was eighteen point seven billion dollars.

The company splits that money into three businesses. Space, meaning launches and contracts with NASA and the military, brought in about four point one billion dollars. Connectivity, which is mostly Starlink, brought in about eleven point four billion dollars. And artificial intelligence, including advertising on X, brought in about three point two billion dollars.

And here is the first surprise. Only one of the three made an operating profit that year. Starlink earned about four point four billion dollars. The space business lost about six hundred and fifty-seven million dollars. The artificial intelligence business lost about six point four billion dollars. Overall, the company reported a net loss of about four point nine billion dollars.

Let me draw the three engines. Here is the space business, the part everyone sees. Here is Starlink, the internet service. Here is artificial intelligence, the newest. Now the arrows. In twenty twenty-five, only Starlink made an operating profit. One engine was carrying the whole ship.

scenes.narration: So let's start with the engine that carries everything.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Starlink sells internet from space. A small dish on a roof talks to satellites flying in low orbit. By the end of September twenty twenty-six, Starlink had about thirteen point six million consumer subscribers, in one hundred and seventy-four countries, territories and other markets. At the end of twenty twenty-three, it had about two point three million.

To serve them, SpaceX flies more than eleven thousand one hundred Starlink satellites. According to the prospectus, SpaceX owns and operates about seventy-five percent of all the active satellites in orbit that can maneuver.

But each customer now pays less than before. Average revenue per subscriber was about ninety-nine dollars a month in twenty twenty-three. In early twenty twenty-six, it was about sixty-six dollars. The company says that is mainly because of international expansion and cheaper plans.

And still, it is very profitable. In the third quarter of twenty twenty-six, the connectivity business earned about two point four billion dollars of operating profit on five point two billion dollars of revenue. By our calculation, that is about forty-five cents of every dollar that comes in.

Let me draw the subscriber climb. Twenty twenty-three, about two point three million. Twenty twenty-four, four point four million. Twenty twenty-five, eight point nine million. And by September twenty twenty-six, thirteen point six million consumers alone. Each bar is a city of customers.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Starlink pays the bills. So what about the rockets?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: SpaceX launches more rockets than anyone. In twenty twenty-five, it flew one hundred and sixty-five Falcon rockets. And according to the prospectus, since twenty twenty-three it has launched more than eighty percent of all the mass sent to orbit by the entire world, every year.

But here is the twist. Of those one hundred and sixty-five launches, only forty-three carried paying customers. The other one hundred and twenty-two carried SpaceX's own Starlink satellites. By our calculation, that is about three out of every four. And for those launches, the space business books no revenue at all, because SpaceX does not charge itself.

What keeps that affordable is reuse. Falcon boosters fly back and land, standing up, on a pad or on a ship at sea. The prospectus counts more than five hundred and seventy successful booster landings. A rocket that lands can fly again.

So why does the space business lose money? The answer is Starship, the giant new rocket. In twenty twenty-five alone, SpaceX spent about three billion dollars on Starship research and development, and it says it has invested more than fifteen billion dollars in it so far. That year, the space business posted an operating loss of about six hundred and fifty-seven million dollars. The prospectus warns that any delay in Starship would limit its growth plans, including computers in orbit.

Rockets also bring in steady government money. In twenty twenty-five, SpaceX launched eleven of the twelve medium and heavy national security missions for the United States, and every crew and cargo mission to the space station for NASA.

Let me draw one year of launches. Here are one hundred and sixty-five rockets. Here, forty-three carry customers, and send money back in. And here, one hundred and twenty-two carry Starlink, and send satellites up, not money. The rocket business works like a delivery truck for the internet business.

scenes.narration: And then, in twenty twenty-six, a third business took over.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In February twenty twenty-six, SpaceX merged with xAI, the maker of the Grok chatbot. Since then the segment has been renamed Super Intelligence. It also includes the social network X, and Cursor, a coding tool SpaceX bought in August at an implied value of sixty billion dollars.

But the biggest money is not from chatbots. It is rent. In May twenty twenty-six, according to the prospectus, SpaceX signed cloud services agreements with Anthropic, another artificial intelligence company, for about three hundred and twenty-five thousand Nvidia graphics chips, at one point two five billion dollars a month through May twenty twenty-nine. After three months, either side can end the deal with ninety days' notice.

Then came the third quarter. SpaceX reported revenue of fourteen point six billion dollars, up from five point six billion dollars a year earlier. Super Intelligence brought in seven point six billion dollars, more than Starlink for the first time. And one single customer, which the filing does not name, accounted for thirty-four point five percent of all revenue in the quarter.

SpaceX even reported a profit that quarter, four point four billion dollars. But that figure was helped by a tax benefit, and by a gain on its stake in another Musk company, The Boring Company. A strong quarter, but not yet proof of a reliable money machine.

And renting out chips costs a fortune up front. In the first nine months of twenty twenty-six, SpaceX spent forty-eight point one billion dollars on capital expenditure. By our calculation, about eighty-three percent of it went to the Super Intelligence business.

Let me draw the third quarter. A bar for rockets, one point eight billion dollars. A bar for Starlink, five point two billion dollars. And a bar for Super Intelligence, seven point six billion dollars. The rocket company now earns its biggest share of revenue from artificial intelligence.

scenes.narration: Which leaves one question. Who is in charge of all this?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Elon Musk. After the offering, according to the prospectus, he held more than eighty percent of the voting power, mostly through special class B shares that carry ten votes each. That makes SpaceX a controlled company under Nasdaq rules.

The prospectus is blunt about it. It says the company is highly dependent on Mr. Musk, that it does not carry key person life insurance on him, and that he does not devote his full time to SpaceX, because he also runs Tesla.

The second big dependence is government. One customer, which the filing does not name, accounted for about twenty-one percent of SpaceX's revenue in twenty twenty-five. Its government contracts are mainly with NASA, the Department of War, the General Services Administration and intelligence agencies.

Let me draw the control panel. Here is SpaceX, with its three businesses. Here are the ordinary shareholders, with their shares. And here is one person, holding more than eighty percent of the votes. Every arrow of control runs through one box.

So how does SpaceX actually make money? Not mainly from rockets. The rocket business has been losing money, because SpaceX is pouring billions into Starship, and most launches carry its own satellites. Starlink makes the operating profit. And now the biggest revenue line is artificial intelligence, much of it from renting out computing power, with one unnamed customer bringing in about a third of the latest quarter's revenue. The lesson is that the most famous part of a company is not always the part that pays. At SpaceX, the rocket is the delivery truck, Starlink is the cash register, and the newest business is a landlord with very large bills. Whether that mix keeps working depends on Starship, on a few big customers, and on one man.
